9. Refactoring the Code: 


9.1 Objective

Now that the Payment Schedule feature is working, it’s time to review our code for:
1. Readability
2. Maintainability
3. Organization

Problem observed:  
The 'main()' method, while not *too* long (~18 lines), contains blocks of code that are “highly related” and serve a single, specific purpose. This makes them prime candidates for extraction into their own methods.




9.2 Refactoring Principles Applied Here

When refactoring a method, look for:
1. Repetitive patterns — duplicated structures that can be generalized.
2. Highly related lines — code that always appears together because it serves one purpose.

In our case:
- No repetition in logic.
- But two distinct, cohesive blocks:
  - Block 1: Printing the Mortgage Summary.
  - Block 2: Printing the Payment Schedule.

These should be separate methods for clarity and reusability.




9.3 Why Extract Methods for These Blocks?

- Improves readability — 'main()' reads like a high-level script:
  '''java
  printMortgage(principal, annualInterest, years);
  printPaymentSchedule(principal, annualInterest, years);
  '''
- Enhances maintainability — changes to printing logic happen in one place.
- Encourages reusability — other programs can call 'printMortgage()' or 'printPaymentSchedule()' if needed.
- Keeps method length under best-practice limits:
  - Ideal: 5–10 lines  
  - Maximum: 20 lines




9.4 Extraction Process

# Step 1 — Printing the Payment Schedule
Original inline code in 'main()':
'''java
System.out.println();
System.out.println("PAYMENT SCHEDULE");
System.out.println("----------------");
for (short month = 1; month <= years * MONTHS_IN_YEAR; month++) {
    double balance = calculateBalance(principal, annualInterest, years, month);
    System.out.println(NumberFormat.getCurrencyInstance().format(balance));
}
'''
Refactored to:
'''java
private static void printPaymentSchedule(int principal, float annualInterest, byte years) {
    System.out.println();
    System.out.println("PAYMENT SCHEDULE");
    System.out.println("----------------");
    for (short month = 1; month <= years * MONTHS_IN_YEAR; month++) {
        double balance = calculateBalance(principal, annualInterest, years, month);
        System.out.println(NumberFormat.getCurrencyInstance().format(balance));
    }
}
'''


# Step 2 — Printing the Mortgage Summary
Original inline code in 'main()':
'''java
double mortgage = calculateMortgage(principal, annualInterest, years);
String mortgageFormatted = NumberFormat.getCurrencyInstance().format(mortgage);
System.out.println();
System.out.println("MORTGAGE");
System.out.println("--------");
System.out.println("Monthly Payments: " + mortgageFormatted);
'''
Refactored to:
'''java
private static void printMortgage(int principal, float annualInterest, byte years) {
    double mortgage = calculateMortgage(principal, annualInterest, years);
    String mortgageFormatted = NumberFormat.getCurrencyInstance().format(mortgage);
    System.out.println();
    System.out.println("MORTGAGE");
    System.out.println("--------");
    System.out.println("Monthly Payments: " + mortgageFormatted);
}
'''




9.5 The Updated Main Method

After extraction, 'main()' becomes:
'''java
public static void main(String[] args) {
    int principal = (int) readNumber("Principal: ", 1000, 1_000_000);
    float annualInterest = (float) readNumber("Annual Interest Rate: ", 1, 30);
    byte years = (byte) readNumber("Period (Years): ", 1, 30);

    printMortgage(principal, annualInterest, years);
    printPaymentSchedule(principal, annualInterest, years);
}
'''
Now:  
- Only 5 lines of actual logic in 'main()'.
- Reads like pseudocode → very easy to follow.




9.6 Full Refactored Code

'''java
package com.codewithmosh;

import java.text.NumberFormat;
import java.util.Scanner;

public class Main {
    final static byte MONTHS_IN_YEAR = 12;
    final static byte PERCENT = 100;

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int principal = (int) readNumber("Principal: ", 1000, 1_000_000);
        float annualInterest = (float) readNumber("Annual Interest Rate: ", 1, 30);
        byte years = (byte) readNumber("Period (Years): ", 1, 30);

        printMortgage(principal, annualInterest, years);
        printPaymentSchedule(principal, annualInterest, years);
    }

    private static void printMortgage(int principal, float annualInterest, byte years) {
        double mortgage = calculateMortgage(principal, annualInterest, years);
        String mortgageFormatted = NumberFormat.getCurrencyInstance().format(mortgage);
        System.out.println();
        System.out.println("MORTGAGE");
        System.out.println("--------");
        System.out.println("Monthly Payments: " + mortgageFormatted);
    }

    private static void printPaymentSchedule(int principal, float annualInterest, byte years) {
        System.out.println();
        System.out.println("PAYMENT SCHEDULE");
        System.out.println("----------------");
        for (short month = 1; month <= years * MONTHS_IN_YEAR; month++) {
            double balance = calculateBalance(principal, annualInterest, years, month);
            System.out.println(NumberFormat.getCurrencyInstance().format(balance));
        }
    }

    public static double readNumber(String prompt, double min, double max) {
        Scanner scanner = new Scanner(System.in);
        double value;
        while (true) {
            System.out.print(prompt);
            value = scanner.nextFloat();
            if (value >= min && value <= max)
                break;
            System.out.println("Enter a value between " + min + " and " + max);
        }
        return value;
    }

    public static double calculateBalance(
            int principal,
            float annualInterest,
            byte years,
            short numberOfPaymentsMade
    ) {
        float monthlyInterest = annualInterest / PERCENT / MONTHS_IN_YEAR;
        float numberOfPayments = years * MONTHS_IN_YEAR;

        double balance = principal
                * (Math.pow(1 + monthlyInterest, numberOfPayments)
                - Math.pow(1 + monthlyInterest, numberOfPaymentsMade))
                / (Math.pow(1 + monthlyInterest, numberOfPayments) - 1);

        return balance;
    }

    public static double calculateMortgage(
            int principal,
            float annualInterest,
            byte years) {

        float monthlyInterest = annualInterest / PERCENT / MONTHS_IN_YEAR;
        float numberOfPayments = years * MONTHS_IN_YEAR;

        double mortgage = principal
                * (monthlyInterest * Math.pow(1 + monthlyInterest, numberOfPayments))
                / (Math.pow(1 + monthlyInterest, numberOfPayments) - 1);

        return mortgage;
    }
}
'''




9.7 Visual Flow Representation

'''
Main()
 ├─ principal = readNumber(...)
 ├─ annualInterest = readNumber(...)
 ├─ years = readNumber(...)
 ├─ printMortgage(principal, annualInterest, years)
 └─ printPaymentSchedule(principal, annualInterest, years)

printMortgage()
 ├─ Calculate mortgage
 ├─ Format currency
 └─ Print "MORTGAGE" section

printPaymentSchedule()
 ├─ For each month:
 │     ├─ calculateBalance()
 │     ├─ format as currency
 │     └─ print balance
'''




9.8 Key Takeaways

- Method extraction improves readability and maintainability.
- Cohesive code blocks should be grouped into their own methods.
- The 'main()' method should act as a high-level coordinator, delegating work to smaller, well-named methods.
- Line count in methods:
  - Ideal: 5–10 lines
  - Max: 20 lines
- IntelliJ (and other IDEs) provide automated refactoring tools that:
  - Detect parameters automatically.
  - Move code into new methods.
  - Replace old code with method calls.




Codes and Other Notes Referred in this Discussion:

package com.codewithmosh;

import java.text.NumberFormat;
import java.util.Scanner;

public class Main {
    final static byte MONTHS_IN_YEAR = 12;
    final static byte PERCENT = 100;

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int principal = (int) readNumber("Principal: ", 1000, 1_000_000);
        float annualInterest = (float) readNumber("Annual Interest Rate: ", 1, 30);
        byte years = (byte) readNumber("Period (Years): ", 1, 30);

        printMortgage(principal, annualInterest, years);
        printPaymentSchedule(principal, annualInterest, years);
    }

    private static void printMortgage(int principal, float annualInterest, byte years) {
        double mortgage = calculateMortgage(principal, annualInterest, years);
        String mortgageFormatted = NumberFormat.getCurrencyInstance().format(mortgage);
        System.out.println();
        System.out.println("MORTGAGE");
        System.out.println("--------");
        System.out.println("Monthly Payments: " + mortgageFormatted);
    }

    private static void printPaymentSchedule(int principal, float annualInterest, byte years) {
        System.out.println();
        System.out.println("PAYMENT SCHEDULE");
        System.out.println("----------------");
        for (short month = 1; month <= years * MONTHS_IN_YEAR; month++) {
            double balance = calculateBalance(principal, annualInterest, years, month);
            System.out.println(NumberFormat.getCurrencyInstance().format(balance));
        }
    }

    public static double readNumber(String prompt, double min, double max) {
        Scanner scanner = new Scanner(System.in);
        double value;
        while (true) {
            System.out.print(prompt);
            value = scanner.nextFloat();
            if (value >= min && value <= max)
                break;
            System.out.println("Enter a value between " + min + " and " + max);
        }
        return value;
    }

    public static double calculateBalance(
            int principal,
            float annualInterest,
            byte years,
            short numberOfPaymentsMade
    ) {
        float monthlyInterest = annualInterest / PERCENT / MONTHS_IN_YEAR;
        float numberOfPayments = years * MONTHS_IN_YEAR;

        double balance = principal
                * (Math.pow(1 + monthlyInterest, numberOfPayments) - Math.pow(1 + monthlyInterest, numberOfPaymentsMade))
                / (Math.pow(1 + monthlyInterest, numberOfPayments) - 1);

        return balance;
    }

    public static double calculateMortgage(
            int principal,
            float annualInterest,
            byte years) {

        float monthlyInterest = annualInterest / PERCENT / MONTHS_IN_YEAR;
        float numberOfPayments = years * MONTHS_IN_YEAR;

        double mortgage = principal
                * (monthlyInterest * Math.pow(1 + monthlyInterest, numberOfPayments))
                / (Math.pow(1 + monthlyInterest, numberOfPayments) - 1);

        return mortgage;
    }
}

10. Summary — Clean Coding & Refactoring Best Practices


10.1 Understanding Clean Coding & Refactoring

In this section, we learned the principles of clean coding and the art of refactoring.

Refactoring is:
The process of restructuring existing code without changing its external behavior.

Purpose:
- Improve readability.
- Enhance maintainability.
- Increase reusability.
- Reduce bugs by making code easier to understand and modify.

Key point: Refactoring never changes *what* the code does, only *how* the code is organized.




10.2 Why Refactoring Matters

As projects grow:
- Methods naturally get longer.
- Responsibilities become mixed.
- Patterns of repetition creep in.

Without refactoring:
- Code becomes harder to read.
- Maintenance costs rise.
- Risk of introducing bugs increases.




10.3 Best Practice — Method Length

- Ideal: 5–10 lines per method.
- Maximum: 20 lines.  
  If a method exceeds this:
  - It’s probably doing too much.
  - It violates the Single Responsibility Principle (SRP).
  - It’s a candidate for extraction into smaller methods.




10.4 How to Identify Refactoring Opportunities

When reviewing code, focus on:

# 1. Repetitive Patterns
- Code blocks that look almost identical except for small variations.
- Example: Multiple input-validation loops in the Mortgage Calculator.

✅ Action: Create a single parameterized method to replace all duplicates.


# 2. Highly Related Statements
- Lines that always occur together and serve one clear purpose.
- Example:  
  - Printing the Mortgage Summary.
  - Printing the Payment Schedule.

✅ Action: Group and extract them into clearly named, separate methods.




10.5 Refactoring Workflow

1. Locate candidates — repetition or high cohesion.
2. Extract method — give it a meaningful name that reflects its purpose.
3. Replace original code with the method call.
4. Test after each change to confirm behavior remains unchanged.




10.6 Benefits of Refactoring

- Readability: Code reads like a story; 'main()' becomes high-level orchestration.
- Maintainability: Easy to make changes without breaking unrelated areas.
- Reusability: Extracted logic can be used elsewhere without duplication.
- Debugging: Smaller methods make isolating problems easier.




10.7 Visual — When to Extract a Method

'''
Before:
main()
 ├── read inputs
 ├── validate inputs
 ├── calculate results
 ├── print summary
 └── print schedule
'''

'''
After:
main()
 ├── principal = readNumber(...)
 ├── rate      = readNumber(...)
 ├── years     = readNumber(...)
 ├── printMortgage(principal, rate, years)
 └── printPaymentSchedule(principal, rate, years)
'''




10.8 Golden Rules to Remember

- Do one thing per method.
- Name methods clearly — names should explain *what* the method does, not *how*.
- Avoid magic numbers — use constants.
- Keep 'main()' clean — it should coordinate, not implement.
- Refactor regularly — don't wait until the code becomes unmanageable.

2. Types of Errors: 

2.1 Introduction

When building Java applications, we inevitably encounter errors — situations where our code either:
- Fails to compile (caught before the program runs), or
- Fails during execution (caught while the program is running).

Understanding the types of errors, their causes, and how to approach fixing them is essential for every Java developer.




2.2 The Two Broad Categories of Errors

| Error Type            | When It Occurs       | Alternate Name          | Typical Cause                                           |
|-----------------------|----------------------|-------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------|
| Compile-time Errors   | During compilation   | Syntax Errors           | Breaking Java's grammar rules or type system            |
| Run-time Errors       | While program is running | Execution Errors    | Invalid operations, unexpected inputs, faulty logic     |


2.2.1 Compile-time Errors (Syntax Errors)

Definition:  
Errors detected by the Java compiler before your program runs, preventing it from producing a '.class' file.

Causes:
- Grammar violations — breaking Java’s syntax rules.
- Type mismatches — assigning incompatible types.
- Missing elements — e.g., semicolons, brackets.
- Invalid references — calling variables or methods that don’t exist.

Characteristics:
- Easy to find — compilers and IDEs (like IntelliJ IDEA) highlight these errors instantly.
- Prevent the program from compiling until fixed.
- Typically shown with red underlines and error messages.

Examples:
'''java
System.out.println("Hello World"  // Missing closing parenthesis and semicolon
int x = "text";  // Type mismatch: assigning String to int
'''

Fixing Strategy:
1. Read the compiler/IDE’s error message carefully — it usually points to where and why the error exists.
2. Correct the syntax or type issue.
3. If unclear:
   - Search the exact error message on Google or StackOverflow.
   - 99% of the time, someone else has faced the same issue, and solutions are readily available.




2.2.2 Run-time Errors

Definition:  
Errors that occur after the program successfully compiles, during execution.

Causes:
- Invalid operations at runtime (e.g., dividing by zero).
- Accessing null objects (NullPointerException).
- Invalid array indexing.
- File operations failing because the file does not exist.
- External factors (e.g., network issues, unavailable resources).

Characteristics:
- Program starts running successfully but crashes or behaves incorrectly at some point.
- Often produce exceptions (error objects) in Java, such as:
  - 'ArithmeticException'
  - 'ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException'
  - 'NullPointerException'
- Can be harder to pinpoint without examining the program’s state at the time of the crash.

Example:
'''java
int x = 10 / 0; // ArithmeticException: / by zero
String s = null;
System.out.println(s.length()); // NullPointerException
'''




2.3 Why Compile-time Errors Are Easier to Fix

- They stop you immediately during compilation.
- Modern IDEs like IntelliJ offer real-time feedback with:
  - Red underlines
  - Tooltips explaining the error
  - Quick-fix suggestions (e.g., auto-importing missing classes)
- Often, the cause is obvious (missing bracket, wrong type, etc.).




2.4 Why Run-time Errors Are Trickier

- The program appears fine until a certain input or condition triggers the error.
- May depend on specific execution paths or data states.
- To track them down, you need to know what was happening in memory when the crash occurred.

Solution:  
Use a Debugger to:
- Run the code step-by-step.
- Inspect variable values at each step.
- See the exact line and condition that causes the failure.




2.5 Debugging as the Key to Fixing Run-time Errors

Debugging involves:
1. Setting breakpoints to pause execution at a certain line.
2. Stepping line-by-line to see the flow of logic.
3. Inspecting variable states to check if they hold expected values.
4. Identifying where and why something went wrong.

In IntelliJ IDEA:
- The debugger panel lets you:
  - Watch variables.
  - Evaluate expressions at runtime.
  - Navigate the call stack to trace the flow.




2.6 Visual Overview

Compile-time Error Cycle:
'''
Write Code → Compile → ❌ Syntax/Type Error → Fix → Compile Again → ✅
'''

Run-time Error Cycle:
'''
Write Code → Compile → Run → ❌ Crash/Unexpected Output → Debug → Fix → ✅
'''




2.7 Key Takeaways

- Compile-time errors:
  - Detected early.
  - Typically easier to fix.
  - Caused by breaking syntax or type rules.
- Run-time errors:
  - Appear only during execution.
  - Often require debugging tools to trace and fix.
- StackOverflow & Google:
  - Valuable resources for troubleshooting unexpected or unclear errors.
- Debugging is an essential skill — it turns “mysterious crashes” into “solvable puzzles”.





Codes and Other Notes Referred in this Discussion:

Compile-time Errors 
Run-time Errors

3. Common Syntax Errors: 


3.1 Introduction

In Java, compile-time errors (often called *syntax errors*) occur when the code you write violates Java’s syntax rules or grammar.  
The compiler detects these issues before the program is run, and they must be fixed before your code can execute.

In this section, we will explore the most common compile-time errors that beginners frequently encounter, why they happen, and how to prevent them.




3.2 Common Compile-Time Errors and Their Causes

# 1. Declaring a Variable Without a Type
Mistake:
'''java
name = "John"; // ❌ Missing data type
'''
Why it happens:
- In languages like Python or JavaScript, variables can be declared without explicitly stating the type.
- In Java, all variables must have a declared type.

Fix:
'''java
String name = "John"; // ✅ Correct — specifies the type
'''
Rule: Always declare a variable with its type ('int', 'String', 'double', etc.).


# 2. Missing Semicolon
Mistake:
'''java
System.out.println("Hello World") // ❌ Missing semicolon
'''
Why it happens:
- Every Java statement (except declarations of code blocks) must end with a semicolon ';'.
- Beginners often forget it after method calls or variable assignments.

Fix:
'''java
System.out.println("Hello World"); // ✅ Correct
'''
Note: You do not add semicolons after:
- Class declarations
- Method declarations
- Control structure headers ('if', 'while', 'for', etc.)


# 3. Calling a Method Without Parentheses
Mistake:
'''java
System.out.println; // ❌ Missing parentheses
'''
Why it happens:
- Beginners sometimes treat methods like variables.
- In Java, all methods require parentheses — even if they have no parameters.

Fix:
'''java
System.out.println(); // ✅ Correct — parentheses indicate a method call
'''


# 4. Forgetting String Quotes
Mistake:
'''java
System.out.println(Hello); // ❌ Missing quotes around string
'''
Why it happens:
- In Java, double quotes ('"') are required for strings.
- Single quotes (''') are for a single character, not strings.

Fix:
'''java
System.out.println("Hello"); // ✅ String literal
System.out.println('H');     // ✅ Character literal
'''


# 5. Misspelling or Incorrectly Capitalizing Variables
Mistake:
'''java
String name = "John";
System.out.println(Name); // ❌ Incorrect capitalization
'''
Why it happens:
- Java is case-sensitive:
  - 'Name' and 'name' are different identifiers.
- Misspellings or wrong capitalization lead to "cannot find symbol" errors.

Fix:
'''java
System.out.println(name); // ✅ Matches variable name exactly
'''


# 6. Using Reserved Keywords as Identifiers
Mistake:
'''java
int class = 5; // ❌ 'class' is reserved
'''
Why it happens:
- Java has reserved keywords (e.g., 'class', 'public', 'static', 'void', etc.).
- These cannot be used as:
  - Variable names
  - Method names
  - Class names

Fix:
'''java
int myClass = 5; // ✅ Choose a different identifier
'''
Tip: Your IDE will highlight reserved keywords automatically.


# 7. Using a Single Equals Sign ('=') in Comparisons
Mistake:
'''java
int x = 0;
if (x = 2) { // ❌ Assignment, not comparison
    System.out.println("Equal");
}
'''
Why it happens:
- In Java, '=' is assignment, not equality check.
- Comparisons use double equals '=='.

Fix:
'''java
if (x == 2) { // ✅ Correct equality check
    System.out.println("Equal");
}
'''
Rule: Always use '==' for primitive equality checks, and '.equals()' for object content comparison.




3.3 Quick Reference Table — Common Syntax Errors

| Mistake | Cause | Fix |
|---------|-------|-----|
| 'name = "John";' | Missing type | 'String name = "John";' |
| Missing ';' | Forgot to end statement | Add ';' at the end |
| 'System.out.println;' | No parentheses | 'System.out.println();' |
| 'System.out.println(Hello);' | Missing quotes | 'System.out.println("Hello");' |
| Wrong capitalization | Java is case-sensitive | Match exact name |
| 'int class = 1;' | Using reserved keyword | Rename variable |
| 'if (x = 2)' | Using assignment instead of comparison | Use '==' for primitives |




3.4 Visual Guide — Error Sources

'''
[Variable Declaration] → Missing Type / Reserved Keyword / Misspelling
[Statements]           → Missing Semicolon
[Method Calls]         → Missing Parentheses
[Strings]               → Missing or Wrong Quotes
[Comparisons]          → Using '=' instead of '=='
'''




3.5 Key Takeaways

- Java enforces strict syntax rules, so minor mistakes stop compilation.
- Case sensitivity means exact spelling matters.
- IDE assistance:
  - IntelliJ highlights issues in real-time.
  - Tooltips often explain exactly what to fix.
- For stubborn errors:
  - Read the error message carefully.
  - Search the exact message on StackOverflow or Google — most likely, it’s already been solved by others.

4. Debugging Java Applications: 



4. Debugging Java Applications — Detailed, Explorative Notes

4.1 Introduction

Debugging is the process of finding and removing errors (bugs) from a program.  
A bug is any defect that causes your program to behave unexpectedly — such as incorrect output, crashes, or skipped logic.

In this tutorial, we will:
- Learn how to debug Java programs using IntelliJ IDEA.
- Explore breakpoints, stepping commands, variable inspection, watches, and call stacks.
- Apply debugging to a real program with a deliberate bug.




4.2 The Example Program

'''java
public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("Start");  
        printNumbers(4); 
        System.out.println("Finish"); 
    }
    
    public static void printNumbers(int limit){
        for(int i = 0; i < limit; i += 2)  // Bug: increments by 2
            System.out.println(i); 
    }
}
'''

Expected Output:
'''
Start
0
1
2
3
4
Finish
'''

Actual Output:
'''
Start
0
2
Finish
'''

Observation: Only even numbers are printed — meaning there’s a bug in the logic.




4.3 Setting a Breakpoint:

Purpose: A breakpoint tells the debugger to pause program execution at a specific line so you can inspect the program’s state.

How to set a breakpoint in IntelliJ:
1. Click in the left gray margin next to the desired code line (e.g., first line inside 'main()').
2. Alternatively, use the keyboard shortcut:  
   - Mac: ⌘ + F8  
   - Windows/Linux: Ctrl + F8
3. Clicking again on the red dot removes the breakpoint.




4.4 Running in Debug Mode

Instead of clicking Run, choose Debug:
- Menu: 'Run → Debug 'Main''
- Shortcut:  
  - Mac: Control + D  
  - Windows/Linux: Shift + F9

When the program starts, it pauses at the breakpoint before executing that line.




4.5 Debugger Interface Overview in IntelliJ

When in debug mode, a Debugger Panel appears:
- Toolbar: Contains stepping and control icons.
- Variables Window: Shows current variables in scope and their values.
- Watches Panel: Lets you manually track specific variables/expressions.
- Frames/Call Stack Window: Shows method call history in reverse order.




4.6 Stepping Through the Code

# 1. Step Over (F8)
Executes the current line without entering into method calls.  
Example: If on 'printNumbers(4)', it will execute the entire method and pause at the next line in 'main()'.

# 2. Step Into (F7)
Executes the current line and enters into the method being called so you can debug it line-by-line.

# 3. Step Out (Shift + F8)
Executes the remaining lines of the current method and returns to the caller.




4.7 Debugging the Bug

1. Start debugging from the beginning — program stops at the breakpoint in 'main()'.
2. Step Over 'System.out.println("Start")' — see '"Start"' in console.
3. Step Over 'printNumbers(4)' — outputs only '0' and '2'.  
   This confirms the bug is inside 'printNumbers()'.
4. Restart debug mode — this time Step Into 'printNumbers(4)'.




4.8 Inspecting Variables

Inside 'printNumbers()':
'''java
for (int i = 0; i < limit; i += 2)
'''
- The 'Variables' window shows:
  - 'limit = 4' (passed from 'main()').
- After the first loop iteration, 'i = 0'.
- Incrementing by 2 ('i += 2') skips odd numbers.




4.9 Adding Watches

If a variable is not in the Variables window:
- Click + in the Watches panel.
- Type the variable/expression name (e.g., 'i').
- Watches update live during execution.

You can remove unnecessary watches to avoid clutter.




4.10 Fixing the Bug

Change:
'''java
i += 2
'''
To:
'''java
i++
'''
Or:
'''java
i += 1
'''
Now the program will print all sequential numbers.




4.11 Restarting Debugging at Specific Points

You don’t have to restart from 'main()' every time:
- Remove the old breakpoint.
- Add a new one where the bug likely occurs (inside 'printNumbers()').
- Use the Resume Program button (▶) to jump directly to that point.




4.12 Skipping the Rest of a Method

When you’ve inspected enough inside a method and want to return to its caller:
- Use Step Out (Shift + F8).




4.13 Understanding the Call Stack (Frames Window)

The Frames Window shows the method call history:
- Last called method is at the top.
- Execution starts in 'main()' → calls 'printNumbers()'.
- Useful for:
  - Seeing how you got to this point.
  - Navigating back up the chain of calls in complex programs.




4.14 Final Corrected Code

'''java
public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("Start");
        printNumbers(4);
        System.out.println("Finish");
    }

    public static void printNumbers(int limit) {
        for (int i = 0; i <= limit; i++)  // fixed increment and <=
            System.out.println(i);
    }
}
'''

Expected Output:
'''
Start
0
1
2
3
4
Finish
'''




4.15 Debugging Process Recap

1. Set Breakpoint where you suspect issues.
2. Run in Debug Mode.
3. Step Through Code with:
   - Step Over (F8)
   - Step Into (F7)
   - Step Out (Shift + F8)
4. Inspect Variables in the Variables Window.
5. Add Watches for critical expressions.
6. Use Call Stack to trace execution paths.
7. Fix the Bug and retest.




4.16 Key Takeaways

- Debugging helps you find the exact cause of a bug instead of guessing.
- Breakpoints save time in large programs by letting you jump directly to problem areas.
- IntelliJ’s Debugger provides:
  - Variable inspection
  - Watches
  - Call Stack navigation
- Debugging is an essential skill — especially when dealing with complex logic or hidden runtime issues.





Codes and Other Notes Referred in this Discussion:

public class Main {
	public static void main(String[] args) {
		System.out.println("Start");  
		printNumbers(4); 
		System.out.println("Finish"); 
	}
	
	public static void printNumbers(int limit){
		for(int i = 0; i < limit; i += 2)
			System.out.println(i); 
	}
	
}

5. Packaging Java Applications: 


5. Packaging Java Applications — Detailed and Comprehensive Notes



5.1 Introduction to Packaging Java Applications

After writing and testing a Java application, the final step before sharing it with others is deployment — making it possible for others to run your program on their machines.

In this context, packaging means taking all the necessary compiled code, resources, and dependencies and bundling them into a single, distributable file.

Scope of This Tutorial
- We focus on console/command-line applications (like those we built in this course).
- We’re not covering packaging web or mobile applications here, because they require additional, platform-specific steps.
- For Java desktop, web, and Android projects, deployment is more complex, often involving tools such as Maven, Gradle, application servers, or app stores.




5.2 Understanding JAR Files

- JAR = Java ARchive
- It's a compressed package format (similar to '.zip') for Java applications.
- Contains:
  - Compiled bytecode files ('.class')
  - Metadata (like 'MANIFEST.MF')
  - Optional resource files (images, text, configuration files)
  - Optional libraries (other '.jar' dependencies)

Purpose:
- Convenient distribution — only one file to share.
- Ensures all required compiled classes are bundled together.
- Can be executed directly if it contains a Main Class.




5.3 Runtime Requirements

For anyone to run your JAR file:
- They must have a Java Runtime Environment (JRE) installed.
- If they don’t:
  - They can download it from [https://java.com/download](https://java.com/download).
- On Windows, capitalization in file names isn’t enforced;  
  on macOS and Linux, capitalization matters ('HelloWorld.jar' ≠ 'helloworld.jar').




5.4 Example Program for Packaging

'''java
package com.codewithmosh;

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("Hello World");
    }
}
'''

This simple program prints '"Hello World"' to the terminal.




5.5 Creating a JAR File in IntelliJ IDEA

# Step 1 — Open Project Structure
1. Go to File → Project Structure.
2. In the left sidebar, select Artifacts.


# Step 2 — Add a New Artifact
- Click '+' to add a new artifact.
- From the dropdown:
  - Choose JAR → From modules with dependencies.


# Step 3 — Configure Module and Main Class
- In the popup:
  1. Select the module — here it's our 'HelloWorld' module.
  2. Click the Main Class selector (magnifying glass icon).
  3. Select your 'Main' class (the one containing 'public static void main').
     - If you have multiple classes with 'main()' methods, they will all appear in the list.
- Optional: Decide how to handle dependencies.
  - In our example, there are none to configure.


# Step 4 — Save the Artifact
- Click OK — now you’ll see a new artifact entry under Artifacts.
- Click OK again to close Project Structure.




5.6 Building the JAR

1. From the Build menu, choose Build Artifacts.
2. Select the artifact you just created (e.g., 'HelloWorld:jar').
3. Choose Build.

Other options in the menu:
- Rebuild — Cleans and builds from scratch (good if something is corrupted).
- Clean — Deletes build output without creating a new build.




5.7 Locating the Generated JAR

- IntelliJ places artifacts in the 'out/artifacts' folder inside your project directory:
  '''
  ProjectRoot/
      out/
          artifacts/
              HelloWorld_jar/
                  HelloWorld.jar
  '''




5.8 Running the JAR File from Terminal

# Step 1 — Open in Terminal
- Right-click on the JAR file in IntelliJ’s Project panel → Open in Terminal.

---

# Step 2 — Run Using 'java -jar'
In the terminal:
'''bash
java -jar HelloWorld.jar
'''

Explanation:
- 'java' → invokes the Java Virtual Machine.
- '-jar' → tells Java you’re running a packaged application.
- 'HelloWorld.jar' → the JAR file to execute.

Example Output:
'''
Hello World
'''




5.9 Visual Representation of the Packaging Workflow

'''
Source Code (.java) → Compilation (javac) → Bytecode (.class) 
→ Package into JAR (with Main-Class manifest) → Distribute JAR 
→ java -jar MyApp.jar → Program Output
'''




5.10 Best Practices for Packaging

- Always define a Main Class in the JAR’s 'MANIFEST.MF' file — this ensures it’s executable without extra parameters.
- Use descriptive artifact names for clarity ('MortgageCalculator.jar' instead of 'Main.jar').
- If your app depends on external libraries:
  - Consider a fat JAR / uber JAR that bundles dependencies into one file.
  - Or distribute the JAR along with a '/lib' directory containing required libraries.
- Test the JAR outside IntelliJ to ensure it runs in a clean environment.




5.11 Key Takeaways

- JAR packaging allows easy distribution and execution of Java console programs.
- The Java Runtime Environment is required to run JAR files.
- IntelliJ’s Artifacts feature simplifies JAR creation:
  - Choose From modules with dependencies.
  - Select the Main Class.
  - Build and run with 'java -jar'.
- Proper packaging means others can run your program without touching your source code.




Codes and Other Notes Referred in this Discussion:

	public static void main(String[] args) {
		System.out.println("Hello World");  
	}	
}

2. Programming Paradigms: 

2.1 Introduction to Programming Paradigms

In computer science, a programming paradigm is a style or methodology of writing and structuring code.  
It defines:
- How problems are approached and modeled.
- How solutions are expressed in code.

Programming paradigms are not programming languages themselves.  
Instead:
- Languages implement one or more paradigms.
- We classify languages by the paradigms they support.




2.2 Examples of Programming Paradigms

Some well-known paradigms include:
1. Procedural Programming — Focuses on sequences of instructions (e.g., C, Pascal).
2. Functional Programming — Treats computation as evaluation of mathematical functions; avoids changing state (e.g., Haskell, parts of Java, JavaScript).
3. Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) — Models problems using objects that encapsulate data and behavior (e.g., Java, C#, Python).
4. Event-Driven Programming — Execution flow determined by user actions/events (e.g., Java Swing, JavaScript UI apps).
5. Logic Programming — Based on formal logic and rule evaluation (e.g., Prolog).
6. Aspect-Oriented Programming (AOP) — Separates cross-cutting concerns (e.g., logging, security).




2.3 Multi-Paradigm vs. Single-Paradigm Languages

- Single-paradigm languages: Support only one style.  
  Example → Smalltalk: Pure object-oriented.
- Multi-paradigm languages: Support multiple styles.  
  Examples:
  - Python
  - Ruby
  - Java (supports OOP + functional features like lambdas and streams)
  - JavaScript




2.4 The Two Most Popular Paradigms Today

Although many paradigms exist, the two most dominant in modern development are:
- Object-Oriented Programming (OOP)
- Functional Programming (FP)




2.5 Object-Oriented Programming — Key Idea

In OOP, everything revolves around objects:
- Object → a self-contained unit that bundles:
  - Data (also called *state*) → stored in fields/attributes.
  - Behavior → implemented as methods/functions that operate on that data.
- Principle: Bring data and its related operations together into a single, reusable entity.

Visual Representation:
'''
+--------------------+
|   BankAccount      |
+--------------------+
| balance: double    |   <-- State (data)
+--------------------+
| deposit(amount)    |   <-- Behavior (method)
| withdraw(amount)   |
+--------------------+
'''




2.6 Functional Programming — Key Idea

In FP:
- Data and behavior are treated as fundamentally different and kept separate.
- Functions:
  - Don’t mutate (change) state.
  - Take input and return new output without side effects (pure functions).
- Code focuses on data transformation using function composition.

Visual Representation:
'''
Data ---> f1() ---> result1 ---> f2() ---> result2 ---> ...
'''



2.7 Solving the Same Problem in Both Paradigms

Example problem: Calculating total salary after tax deduction.

OOP approach:
'''java
Employee e = new Employee("John", 50000);
e.calculateNetSalary();
'''
- The 'Employee' object knows how to calculate its own net salary.

FP approach:
'''java
calculateNetSalary(employeeData);
'''
- A pure function takes raw employee data and returns the computed net salary.

Result: Same solution, different code structure and thought process.



2.8 Which Paradigm is Better?

Answer: It depends — there’s no universal “best” paradigm.

- Some developers love one paradigm and use it for everything (not always ideal).
- Others dislike a paradigm because they misunderstood or misapplied it.
  - Example: Many who “hate” OOP never truly learned its principles.
- OOP can be complex — many books and courses fail to explain it effectively.




2.9 Real-World Suitability (General Guidelines)

- OOP:
  - Well-suited for graphical user interfaces (GUIs).
  - Common in game development.
  - Helpful when modeling complex real-world entities.
- FP:
  - Ideal for high-reliability systems.
  - Works well with data pipelines where data is passed and transformed.
- Event-Driven:
  - Great for UI programming where actions are triggered by events.

> Note: These are guidelines, not hard rules. Context matters.




2.10 Mixing Paradigms

In a single application, you might:
- Use event-driven programming for the UI layer.
- Use OOP for domain/business logic.
- Use FP for data processing modules.

Why?
- No paradigm is perfect for all scenarios.
- The best choice is context-driven and problem-focused.




2.11 Core Software Engineering Principle
> “There’s no one-size-fits-all in software engineering.”

- Best language? Depends on the problem, constraints, and budget.
- Best framework? Depends on team skill set, project requirements, performance needs.
- Dogmatically applying one paradigm to all problems can lead to poor solutions.




2.12 Problem-Solving Comes First

Many developers:
- Get too attached to a tool/language/paradigm.
- Forget that the main goal is solving problems.

True problem solving means:
1. Clearly define the problem.
2. Identify possible solutions.
3. Compare trade-offs considering:
   - Project context
   - Constraints (time, budget, resources)
4. Choose the most fit-for-purpose approach.




2.13 Key Takeaways

- Programming paradigms are styles of structuring solutions — not languages themselves.
- Most modern languages (Java, Python, JavaScript) are multi-paradigm.
- OOP = unify data & behavior in objects.  
  FP = keep data & behavior separate and use pure functions.
- Use the right paradigm for the right problem.
- Stay flexible — avoid falling in love with one solution and applying it blindly.
- Context and constraints matter more than personal preference.

Functional
Object-oriented

Object-oriented:

Methods(Behaviour)

3. Benefits Of Object-oriented Programming: 

3.1 Introduction

Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) is a programming paradigm based on the concept of objects — self-contained entities that combine data (state) and behavior (methods/functions that operate on the data).  
These objects interact with each other to accomplish tasks within an application, much like how components in a real-world system work together.




3.2 Real-World Analogy — The Car Example

Think of a car:
- It is composed of hundreds or thousands of smaller parts, each functioning as an object:
  - Engine
  - Transmission
  - Wheels
  - Brakes
  - Sensors
- Each of these parts:
  - Is reusable in other cars (e.g., a specific tire model used in multiple vehicles).
  - Is replaceable — if a part malfunctions, it can be removed and swapped with another.

How this applies to OOP:
- A software application is similar — it consists of collaborating objects.
- If an object in the program fails, we can:
  - Fix that object without touching unrelated parts.
  - Replace it with another object (like swapping a faulty component in a car).




3.3 Core Benefits of OOP

# 1. Reduced Complexity
- Large, complex applications can be broken down into smaller, more manageable objects.
- Each object focuses on one responsibility (Single Responsibility Principle).
- Easier to understand, design, and reason about smaller parts.

Visual Representation:
'''
[Whole App]
   ↓ Break into ↓
[User Interface]  [Business Logic]  [Database Layer]
   ↓ Further ↓
[UI Button] [Login Manager] [SQL Query Builder]
'''


# 2. Easier Maintenance
- If there’s a bug, you can focus only on the faulty object.
- No need to sift through the entire application.
- Encourages modularity:
  - Code changes in one object don’t impact other parts (if well-encapsulated).
- Enables plug-and-play replacement of components.


# 3. Code Reuse
- Once an object is designed, coded, and tested, it can be reused:
  - In different parts of the same application.
  - In other applications entirely.
- This is especially valuable when building utility classes or modular libraries.

Example:
- An ImageFilter object in an image editing app:
  - Can be reused in:
    - Desktop image editors
    - Mobile photo editing apps
    - Online web-based editors
- Eliminates duplication of effort.


# 4. Faster Development
- Reuse of tested objects → less time spent reinventing the wheel.
- Teams can work on different objects in parallel without interfering with each other’s code.
- Libraries and frameworks built with OOP provide pre-made components that accelerate development.




3.4 Addressing Misconceptions

- Some developers claim OOP’s benefits are purely theoretical because:
  - They’ve never successfully reused or replaced objects in practice.
- The likely reason:  
  - OOP was not applied correctly.
  - Poor design can make objects tightly coupled, defeating OOP’s flexibility.

> Lesson: If a tool doesn’t work for you, it doesn’t necessarily mean the tool is bad — you might just be using it incorrectly.




3.5 Comparison with Functional Programming

- Advocates of Functional Programming (FP) argue that FP also delivers:
  - Reduced complexity
  - Easier maintenance
  - Reusability
  - Faster development
- This is true — both paradigms offer benefits, but neither is a one-size-fits-all solution.




3.6 The Balanced Approach

- Learn both paradigms:
  - OOP for problems best modeled as interacting entities.
  - FP for problems centered on data transformation and immutability.
- Choose the paradigm based on the problem, context, and constraints.




3.7 Visual Summary — OOP Benefits

'''
┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
│   BENEFITS OF OBJECT-ORIENTED PROG  │
├─────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 1. Reduced Complexity               │
│ 2. Easier Maintenance               │
│ 3. Code Reuse                       │
│ 4. Faster Development               │
└─────────────────────────────────────┘
'''




3.8 Key Takeaways

- OOP = Objects (State + Behavior) working together.
- Breaks down large problems into manageable, modular parts.
- Enables component replacement without breaking the whole system.
- Encourages reuse, reducing development effort and speeding up delivery.
- Neither OOP nor FP is always the best choice — context determines the right tool.

4. Course Structure: 



4. Course Structure — Detailed, Structured, and Immersive Notes


4.1 Purpose of the Course Structure

The way this course is designed ensures:
- A progressive learning path — from fundamental OOP concepts to their advanced applications.
- A blend of theory and practical refactoring exercises to develop real-world coding skills.
- Layered reinforcement — each section builds upon the previous one so concepts stick.




4.2 Overview of the Learning Flow

# 1. Classes — The Building Blocks of OOP
- Why this comes first:  
  Classes are the foundation of Object-Oriented Programming.  
  Without them, concepts like inheritance or polymorphism have no context.
  
- What you’ll learn:
  - Definition of a class.
  - Why we need classes in Java.
  - How to create and instantiate them.
  - Real-world analogies to visualize objects and their classes.
  
- Why it matters:  
  A solid understanding of classes sets the stage for all other OOP principles.

	
# 2. First Two OOP Principles — Encapsulation & Abstraction
- Encapsulation:
  - The idea of wrapping data and related methods together.
  - Protecting the state of an object from unintended interference.
  - Using access modifiers ('private', 'public', etc.) to control access.

- Abstraction:
  - Hiding unnecessary details while exposing only what’s essential.
  - Achieved through abstract classes and interfaces (at this stage conceptually).

- Teaching approach:
  - Metaphors (real-life examples to simplify concepts).
  - Code illustrations to clarify their application in practice.
  
- Outcome:  
  By the end, you’ll be able to both identify and implement encapsulation and abstraction in your own code.


# 3. Applying Principles — Refactoring the Mortgage Calculator
- You’ll revisit the Mortgage Calculator Project from Part 1.
- The goal: Refactor the procedural code into clean, maintainable, object-oriented code.
- Why this is critical:
  - Shows how to apply theory in a real-world context.
  - You’ll learn to break down messy, tightly coupled logic into modular, reusable classes.
  - This is a core skill that even many experienced developers lack.


# 4. The Other Two OOP Principles — Inheritance & Polymorphism
- Inheritance:
  - Mechanism for creating hierarchies and reusing code.
  - Enables shared behavior across related classes.

- Polymorphism:
  - Ability for different classes to respond differently to the same method call.
  - Makes systems more flexible and extensible.

- Outcome:  
  You’ll learn when and how to use these features without falling into common misuse patterns.


# 5. Interfaces — Powerful but Understood by Few
- Why important:
  - Interfaces are one of the most powerful features of Java OOP.
  - Sadly, they’re also one of the most misunderstood.
  
- Key lessons:
  - Understanding coupling — how tightly classes depend on each other.
  - Problems caused by tight coupling.
  - How interfaces reduce dependencies, making code more modular and testable.
  
- Hands-on:  
  - Implementing interfaces in real examples.
  - Designing code that’s easy to modify and extend.




4.3 How This Structure Benefits You

By following this sequence:
- You start with the basics (classes).
- Then layer in principles (encapsulation, abstraction).
- Immediately apply them through refactoring.
- Add advanced OOP tools (inheritance, polymorphism).
- Finally, master interfaces to design loosely coupled systems.

This path ensures you:
- Build deep conceptual understanding.
- Gain practical skills that transfer to real-world Java development.
- Are better equipped to read and understand Java SDK classes and frameworks.

'''

    ↓

    ↓
[Strong OOP Foundation]
'''

- The course is built to gradually increase complexity.
- Each section is both self-contained and connected to the larger OOP picture.
- By the end, you’ll have:
  - Solid OOP fundamentals.
  - Practical experience in refactoring toward clean architecture.
  - Insight into best practices for using OOP in any Java project.

Classes: 

1. Introduction: 





1.1 Why Classes Matter in OOP

In Object-Oriented Programming (OOP), classes are the fundamental building blocks.  
They serve as blueprints for creating objects — the actual entities that exist and interact inside a program.

Think of classes as design specifications or architectural blueprints:
- The class defines the structure and behavior of an object.
- The object is a specific instance of that class.

Without classes:
- We’d lose OOP’s organizational power.
- Codebases would be harder to maintain, extend, or understand.




1.2 Purpose of This Section

In this section, you will:
- Learn what classes are, and why we use them.
- Explore how to declare and implement classes in Java.
- Understand key OOP principles:
  - Encapsulation — bundling data and methods, controlling access.
  - Abstraction — exposing only what’s necessary, hiding the rest.
- Gain practical experience with:
  - Constructors (special methods for object creation).
  - Getters & Setters (controlled data access and modification).
  - Method Overloading (multiple methods with the same name but different parameters).
- Prepare for hands-on application in a real-world refactoring project in the next section.




1.3 Key OOP Principles to be Covered

# Encapsulation
- Definition: Wrapping data (fields) and methods that operate on that data inside the same unit — the class.
- Purpose: Protects internal object state from unintended interference.
- Tools in Java:
  - Access modifiers ('private', 'public', 'protected').
  - Getters and setters to manage controlled access.

Analogy: A remote control has buttons (methods) you can press, but you can’t directly mess with the internal electronics (private data).


# Abstraction
- Definition: Hiding complex internal logic and exposing only the essential interface.
- Purpose: Reduces complexity for the end-user of a class.
- Tools in Java:
  - Abstract classes
  - Interfaces
  - Public methods that mask detailed implementation.

Analogy: When you drive a car, you use the pedals and steering wheel without worrying about the internal engine mechanics.


# Constructors
- Definition: Special methods automatically called when creating an object.
- Purpose: Initialize the object’s state.
- Varieties:
  - Default constructors
  - Parameterized constructors
  - Overloaded constructors


# Getters & Setters
- Getters: Provide read-only access to private fields.
- Setters: Control how data is updated, often including validation logic.
- They maintain encapsulation by controlling what the outside world can change.


# Method Overloading
- Definition: Multiple methods in the same class sharing the same name but differing in parameter type, number, or order.
- Purpose: Improves code readability and flexibility.
- Example:
  '''java
  void print(String message) { ... }
  void print(int number) { ... }
  void print(String message, int count) { ... }
  '''




1.4 The Bigger Picture

- The concepts in this section are core OOP skills you’ll reuse in every Java project.
- Understanding classes means understanding how Java’s standard libraries (Java Development Kit) are built.
- These skills are directly transferable to other OOP languages (C#, Python, C++).




1.5 Recommended Learning Approach

- Follow along with code examples — don’t just read, type them out yourself.
- Experiment by modifying examples:
  - Change access modifiers.
  - Add extra constructors.
  - Overload methods with different parameters.
- Take notes on:
  - Syntax.
  - Practical uses.
  - Real-world analogies.




1.6 Visual Representation

Class as a Blueprint → Objects as Instances
'''
Blueprint: Class "Car"
+--------------+
| Fields:      |
|  - color     |
|  - speed     |
+--------------+
| Methods:     |
|  + drive()   |
|  + brake()   |
+--------------+

Objects Created:
Car myCar = new Car();
Car yourCar = new Car();
'''

Both 'myCar' and 'yourCar' follow the same blueprint but may have different state values ('color', 'speed').




1.7 Key Takeaways

- Classes are the foundation of OOP in Java.
- They combine state (fields) and behavior (methods) in one unit.
- This section covers:
  - Encapsulation
  - Abstraction
  - Constructors
  - Getters/Setters
  - Method Overloading
- You’ll apply all these concepts in the next section’s project.

2. Classes and Objects: 

2.1 Introduction

Before we dive into coding, it’s important to clearly distinguish between classes and objects.

- These two terms are often used interchangeably, but they are not the same thing.
- Understanding their difference is fundamental to mastering Object-Oriented Programming (OOP).




2.2 Class vs. Object — Core Definitions

| Concept | Meaning                                                                                        | Analogy                                        |
|---------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------|
| Class   | A blueprint or template that defines the structure (fields) and behavior (methods) of objects. | The architectural plan of a building.          |
| Object  | An instance of a class — a real, existing entity created using the class blueprint.            | The actual building constructed from the plan. |




2.3 Example — The 'Car' Class

A class describes what a Car *is* and *can do*.

Fields (State)
- 'started' → Whether the car is running or not ('boolean').
- 'currentSpeed' → Current speed of the car ('int' or 'double').
- 'currentGear' → Current gear position ('int').

Methods (Behavior)
- 'start()' → Starts the car.
- 'stop()' → Stops the car.
- 'brake()' → Slows the car down.
- 'changeGear()' → Modifies 'currentGear'.

How it works:
- These fields store the current state of a car object.
- The methods change or use this state.
- Example:
  '''java
  car.changeGear(3); 
  // Updates 'currentGear' field from, say, 2 → 3
  '''




2.4 Creating Objects from a Class

When you define the 'Car' class:
'''java
Car car1 = new Car();
Car car2 = new Car();
Car car3 = new Car();
'''
- All objects ('car1', 'car2', 'car3') share the same structure (same fields/methods).
- Each object:
  - Occupies a separate memory location.
  - Maintains its own state.
  - Can behave independently from the others.

Example of state independence:
| Object  | Current Gear | Current Speed |
|---------|--------------|---------------|
| car1    | 2            | 40 km/h       |
| car2    | 4            | 90 km/h       |
| car3    | 1            | 15 km/h       |




2.5 UML Representation

We can use UML (Unified Modeling Language) to represent classes and objects visually.

# UML for 'Car':
'''
+---------------------+
|       Car           |
+---------------------+
| - started: boolean  |
| - currentSpeed: int |
| - currentGear: int  |
+---------------------+
| + start()           |
| + stop()            |
| + brake()           |
| + changeGear()      |
+---------------------+
'''

> UML is a visual language for showing classes, their fields, methods, and relationships.  
> While it’s a much bigger topic on its own, we will use simple UML diagrams here to improve clarity.




2.6 Another Example — The 'Lamp' Class

State (Field):
- 'isOn' ('boolean') → Represents whether the lamp is turned on.

Behavior (Methods):
- 'turnOn()' → Sets 'isOn = true'.
- 'turnOff()' → Sets 'isOn = false'.

UML:
'''
+--------------+
|    Lamp      |
+--------------+
| - isOn: boolean |
+--------------+
| + turnOn()   |
| + turnOff()  |
+--------------+
'''




2.7 Practice Question — The 'TV' Class

States (Possible Fields):
- 'isOn' ('boolean') → Power state of the TV.
- 'currentVolume' ('int') → Current volume level.
- 'currentChannel' ('int' or 'String') → The channel being watched.

Behaviors (Possible Methods):
- 'turnOn()', 'turnOff()'
- 'increaseVolume()', 'decreaseVolume()'
- 'changeChannel()'




2.8 Software-Based Example — The 'TextBox' Class

We don’t always model physical objects — many objects are purely software-based.

States (Fields):
- 'text' ('String') → The content inside the text box.
- 'maxLength' ('int') → Max number of characters allowed.
- 'width' ('int') → Width in pixels.
- 'isFocused' ('boolean') → Whether the text box is active.
- 'isDisabled' ('boolean') → Whether the user can type in it.

Behaviors (Methods):
- 'setText(String newText)' → Updates the content.
- 'clear()' → Removes all text.
- 'enable()', 'disable()' → Change usability state.
- 'focus()' → Brings the text box into active view.




2.9 Key Differences Between Classes and Objects

| Aspect        | Class                                       | Object                                |
|---------------|---------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------|
| Definition    | Blueprint/template                          | Instance of a class                   |
| Existence     | Exists in code only until instantiated      | Exists in memory when created         |
| State         | Defines possible states                     | Has its own actual state              |
| Behavior      | Defines possible behaviors                  | Executes behaviors, affects its state |




2.10 Visual Summary

'''
[Blueprint: Class]
   ↓
[Instance: Object]
   ↓
[Has State + Behavior]
'''
Example Flow:
- Define 'Car' class → Create 'car1' → Call 'car1.start()' → Change its state ('started = true').




2.11 Key Takeaways

- A Class defines structure and behavior but has no actual state until instantiated.
- An Object is created from a class and has its own independent state in memory.
- Fields store state, methods define behavior.
- UML is a useful visual tool for representing class design.
- Real-world or purely software-based entities can both be modeled as classes in Java.




Codes and Other Notes Referred in this Discussion:

Car
 - Fields
   - started
   - currentSpeed
   - currentGear
 - Methods
   - start()
   - stop()
   - brake()
   - changeGear()

3. Creating Classes: 


3.1 Introduction

In Java, classes are the blueprints from which objects are created.  
They define:
- State → Stored in fields (variables inside the class).
- Behavior → Implemented as methods (functions inside the class).

In this tutorial, we will:
- Learn how to create a new class from scratch.
- Understand naming conventions.
- Explore access modifiers ('public', 'private', etc.).
- Add fields and methods to a class.
- Use the 'this' keyword for clarity.




3.2 Project Setup

We’ll create a new 'TextBox' class alongside our existing 'Main' class.

Steps in IntelliJ IDEA:
1. Open the Project Panel.
2. Expand the 'src' folder — your main package lives here.
3. Right-click inside the package → New → Java Class.
4. Name it 'TextBox' using PascalCase (capitalize the first letter of every word).
5. Ensure Kind is set to Class.




3.3 Java Naming Conventions

- Classes → PascalCase
  - Example: 'TextBox', 'Car', 'BankAccount'
- Fields & Methods → camelCase
  - Example: 'text', 'setText()', 'clearText()'
- Constants → UPPERCASE_WITH_UNDERSCORES
  - Example: 'MAX_LENGTH'

Why follow conventions?
- Improves readability.
- Keeps your code consistent with Java community standards.




3.4 Access Modifiers

At the top of our new file:
'''java
public class TextBox {
    ...
}
'''
- 'public' → This class can be accessed from anywhere in the project.
- Access modifiers control:
  - Visibility of classes, fields, and methods.
  - Encapsulation (we’ll explore this deeply later).




3.5 Adding Members to the Class

We’ll give our 'TextBox' one field and two methods.


# Field — Representing the State
'''java
public String text;
'''
- 'public' → Visible to other classes (we’ll refine this later for encapsulation).
- 'String' → Stores text input inside the text box.
- 'text' → Variable name (camelCase).


# Method 1 — 'setText()'
Purpose: Assign a new value to the 'text' field.

'''java
public void setText(String text) {
    this.text = text;
}
'''

 Key points:
- 'public' → Accessible from outside the class.
- 'void' → Returns nothing.
- Parameter: '(String text)' — The new value.
- 'this' keyword:
  - Refers to the current object.
  - Used here to disambiguate between the parameter 'text' and the field 'text'.
  - Without 'this' → 'text = text;' is unclear and does nothing useful.


# Method 2 — 'clear()'
Purpose: Remove all text from the 'TextBox'.

'''java
public void clear() {
    text = "";
}
'''
- No parameters.
- Sets the 'text' field to an empty string.
- No need for 'this' here because there’s no naming conflict.




3.6 The 'this' Keyword in Detail

- Refers to the current instance of the class.
- Commonly used:
  1. To resolve naming conflicts between parameters and fields.
  2. To pass the current object as an argument to another method.
  3. To call another constructor from within a constructor.

Example:
'''java
public void setText(String text) {
    this.text = text; // 'this.text' = field, 'text' = parameter
}
'''




3.7 Inherited Methods

When we type 'this.' inside our class, IntelliJ shows:
- Our own members ('text', 'setText()', 'clear()').
- Extra methods like 'clone()', 'equals()', 'toString()'.

Why?
- Every class in Java automatically inherits from 'java.lang.Object'.
- This provides common functionality to all Java objects.
- We’ll explore inheritance in detail in the next section.




3.8 Final 'TextBox' Class

'''java
package com.codewithmosh;

public class TextBox {
    public String text;  // Field (state)

    public void setText(String text) {  // Method (behavior)
        this.text = text;
    }

    public void clear() {  // Method (behavior)
        text = "";
    }
}
'''




3.9 Example 'Main' Class

'''java
package com.codewithmosh;

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // We'll create TextBox objects here in the next tutorial
    }
}
'''




3.10 Visual UML Representation

'''
+-------------------------------+
|           TextBox             |
+-------------------------------+
| text : String                 |
+-------------------------------+
| setText(text: String) : void  |
| clear() : void                |
+-------------------------------+
'''
- Attributes (fields) at the top.
- Methods (behaviors) below.




3.11 Notes on Public Fields

- Declaring fields as 'public' is not recommended in real-world applications.
- We will later use private fields + getters/setters to:
  - Protect data.
  - Maintain encapsulation.
  - Add validation logic.

For now, 'public' is used for learning purposes and gradual introduction to OOP best practices.




3.12 Key Takeaways

- Each class should be in its own '.java' file.
- PascalCase for class names, camelCase for variables/methods.
- 'this' helps resolve naming conflicts and refers to the current object.
- Classes can contain:
  - Fields (state)
  - Methods (behavior)
- All Java classes implicitly extend 'Object'.








Codes and Other Notes Referred in this Discussion:

public class Main{
	public static void main(String[] args){
	
	}
}



TextBox.java:

  public String text;  //Field

  public void setText(String text) {  //Method
    this.text = text;
  }

  }
}

4. Creating Objects: 

4.1 Introduction

In the previous lesson, we defined the 'TextBox' class — a blueprint describing what a text box *is* and *can do*.  
Now, we will instantiate this class to create real objects in memory and explore:
- How to declare and initialize objects.
- How to use the 'new' operator.
- How to access members (fields & methods) of an object.
- Potential pitfalls like 'NullPointerException' and how to avoid them.
- How multiple objects from the same class operate independently.




4.2 Creating an Object

In Java, we create an object by:
1. Declaring a variable of the class type.
2. Using the 'new' operator to allocate memory and call the class’s constructor.

Example:
'''java
var textBox1 = new TextBox();  
// Equivalent to: TextBox textBox1 = new TextBox();
'''
- 'new TextBox()': Instantiates the class → allocates memory and initializes it.
- The resulting object is assigned to 'textBox1'.




4.3 Using 'var' for Type Inference

# Before:
'''java
TextBox textBox1 = new TextBox();
'''
- The type 'TextBox' is repeated twice — visually noisy.

# After:
'''java
var textBox1 = new TextBox();
'''
- 'var' → Lets the Java compiler infer the type based on the right-hand side.
- This makes code cleaner and shorter.
- Important: This 'var' in Java is not dynamic typing (like JavaScript's 'var').
  - In Java: Once inferred, the variable type cannot change.
  - In JavaScript: 'var' allows reassignment to different types (not allowed in Java).




4.4 Accessing Class Members

We use the dot operator ('.') to:
- Call methods.
- Access fields.

Example:
'''java
textBox1.setText("Box 1");  
System.out.println(textBox1.text);
'''
Output:
'''
Box 1
'''




4.5 Default Values and 'null'

If we remove 'setText()' and directly print:
'''java
System.out.println(textBox1.text);
'''
We get:
'''
null
'''
Reason:
- 'String' is a reference type (non-primitive).
- By default, uninitialized reference fields are set to 'null'.

Danger of 'null':
- Calling a method on a 'null' reference causes a 'NullPointerException'.
  
Example:
'''java
System.out.println(textBox1.text.toUpperCase()); // ❌ Will crash
'''

Error:
'''
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.NullPointerException
'''
- This means we tried to call a method on an object that does not exist in memory.




4.6 Preventing 'NullPointerException'

We can initialize the field directly in the class:
'''java
public String text = "";
'''
- Now, 'text' will never be 'null' — instead, it starts as an empty string ('""').
- If 'toUpperCase()' is called before assigning a value, it will work and return '""'.




4.7 Creating Multiple Independent Objects

Example:
'''java
var textBox1 = new TextBox();
textBox1.setText("Box 1");

var textBox2 = new TextBox();
textBox2.setText("Box 2");

System.out.println(textBox1.text); // Box 1
System.out.println(textBox2.text); // Box 2
'''

# Observation:
- Both 'textBox1' and 'textBox2' have the same structure but different states.
- They exist independently in memory.




4.8 Memory Model Overview

When you create:
'''java
var textBox1 = new TextBox();
'''
In memory:
- 'textBox1' (variable) lives on the stack.
- The actual 'TextBox' object lives on the heap.
- The variable holds a reference (memory address) to the object.

Visualization:
'''
Stack                  Heap
------                 --------------------
textBox1   --->   [ TextBox object ]
                   text: "Box 1"
                   methods: setText(), clear()
'''




4.9 Final Example Code

'''java
package com.codewithmosh;

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        var textBox1 = new TextBox();
        textBox1.setText("Box 1");
        System.out.println(textBox1.text); // Box 1

        var textBox2 = new TextBox();
        textBox2.setText("Box 2");
        System.out.println(textBox2.text); // Box 2
    }
}
'''

'TextBox' class:
'''java
package com.codewithmosh;

public class TextBox {
    public String text = ""; // Prevents null

    public void setText(String text) {
        this.text = text;
    }

    public void clear() {
        text = "";
    }
}
'''




4.10 UML Representation

'''
+----------------------+
|      TextBox         |
+----------------------+
| text : String = ""   |
+----------------------+
| setText(text:String) |
| clear()              |
+----------------------+
'''




4.11 Key Takeaways

- Instantiating a class creates an object in heap memory.
- 'var' can reduce verbosity but does not allow type changes in Java.
- Uninitialized reference fields default to 'null' → be careful to avoid 'NullPointerException'.
- Initializing fields (e.g., with an empty string) prevents crashes and ensures predictable behavior.
- Multiple objects from the same class have independent states.

		var textbox1 = new TextBox(); //Initially, TextBox textbox1 = new TextBox();
		textbox1.setText("Box 1")
		System.out.println(textbox1.text); //Box 1
	
	}

5. Memory Allocation: 


5.1 Introduction

Understanding memory allocation is crucial in Java because it:
- Explains how and where your data is stored.
- Clarifies the difference between primitive types and reference types.
- Helps you anticipate behavior when multiple variables refer to the same object.
- Highlights Java’s automatic memory management through Garbage Collection.

When we create variables and objects in Java, they are stored in two main memory areas:
1. Heap Memory → Stores objects and their instance variables.
2. Stack Memory → Stores:
   - Primitive type variables.
   - References (addresses) pointing to objects in the heap.
   - Local variables created inside methods.




5.2 Heap vs Stack — Core Concepts

| Aspect             | Heap                                                                                | Stack                                      |
|--------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------|
| Purpose            | Stores objects and their associated instance data.                                  | Stores method call frames, local variables, and references to objects. |
| Lifespan           | Objects live until no references point to them → then removed by Garbage Collector. | Data is removed as soon as the method ends. |
| Access             | Shared globally across threads (needs synchronization in multi-threaded programs).  | Local to a thread/method call — not shared between threads. |
| Storage            | Actual objects.                                                                     | Primitive values or addresses (references) pointing to heap objects. |




5.3 What Happens When We Create a New Object

Consider the code:
'''java
var textBox1 = new TextBox();
'''

# Step-by-Step Execution:
1. Right-hand side ('new TextBox()'):
   - A new 'TextBox' object is created on the heap.
   - Let’s say it’s stored at memory address '100'.

2. Left-hand side ('var textBox1'):
   - A variable 'textBox1' is created on the stack.
   - It holds the reference (address) of the object — in this example, '100'.

Diagram:
'''
Stack                Heap
------               --------------------------
textBox1  --->   [ TextBox Object @ 100 ]
                   text: ""
                   setText()
                   clear()
'''




5.4 Primitive Types vs Reference Types

- Primitive Types: Store the value directly in the stack.
  '''java
  int number = 10; // Stack: number = 10
  '''
- Reference Types: Store a reference (address) in the stack that points to the actual object in the heap.
  '''java
  String name = "John"; // Stack: name = address 200 → Heap: "John"
  '''




5.5 Multiple References to the Same Object

Consider:
'''java
var textBox1 = new TextBox();
var textBox2 = textBox1; // No new object created
'''

# What Happens:
- 'textBox1' and 'textBox2' are two different variables on the stack.
- Both store the same memory address (e.g., '100') of the same object in the heap.
- This means they are aliases — two names for the same object.

Diagram:
'''
Stack                 Heap
------                --------------------------
textBox1 --->     [ TextBox Object @ 100 ]
textBox2 ---^      text: ""
                  setText()
                  clear()
'''




5.6 Proof — Modifying Through One Reference Affects the Other

'''java
textBox2.setText("Hello World");
System.out.println(textBox1.text);
'''
Output:
'''
Hello World
'''
- Because both variables refer to the same heap object, changes via one reference are visible through the other.




5.7 Memory Deallocation — Garbage Collection

# Automatic in Java:
- Unlike C++, Java has no 'delete' keyword.
- Memory cleanup is handled by the Garbage Collector (GC).
- GC runs in the background and removes heap objects that no longer have any references.

Example Flow:
1. Inside 'main()':
   - Both 'textBox1' and 'textBox2' exist on the stack.
   - They both point to the same heap object.

2. After 'main()' ends:
   - Both variables go out of scope and are removed from the stack.
   - Now, the heap object has no references pointing to it.

3. Garbage Collection:
   - GC detects the object is unreachable.
   - Object is removed from heap → memory is reclaimed.




5.8 Visualizing Memory Life Cycle

# Step 1 — Creation
'''
Stack                Heap
------               --------------------------
textBox1  --->  [TextBox @ 100]
                   text: ""
'''

# Step 2 — Copying the Reference
'''
Stack                Heap
------               --------------------------
textBox1  --->  [TextBox @ 100]
textBox2  ---^      text: ""
'''

# Step 3 — Modifying via One Reference
'''
textBox2.setText("Hello World");

Stack                Heap
------               --------------------------
textBox1  --->  [TextBox @ 100]
textBox2  ---^      text: "Hello World"
'''

# Step 4 — After Method Ends
'''
Stack                Heap
------               --------------------------
(empty)          [TextBox @ 100] ← No references → Marked for GC
'''




5.9 Best Practices

- Be careful when assigning one reference to another — you may unintentionally modify the same object.
- Initialize reference fields to safe values (e.g., '""' for 'String') to avoid 'NullPointerException'.
- Avoid unnecessary object creation — reuse objects when appropriate.
- Don’t rely on exact timing of garbage collection — Java decides when to run GC.




5.10 Example Code

'''java
package com.codewithmosh;

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        var textBox1 = new TextBox();
        var textBox2 = textBox1;

        textBox2.setText("Hello World");
        System.out.println(textBox1.text); // Output: Hello World
    }
}
'''




5.11 Key Takeaways

- Stack = method calls + primitives + object references.
- Heap = actual objects.
- Multiple variables can reference the same object in heap.
- Java automatically manages memory via Garbage Collection.
- Understanding memory allocation helps avoid bugs, especially when aliasing references.




Codes and Other Notes Referred in this Discussion:

Heap
Stack 


Main.java:

public class Main{
	public static void main(String[] args){
		var textbox1 = new TextBox(); 
		var textbox2 = textbox1; 
		textbox2.setText("Hello World")
		System.out.println(textbox1.text); //Hello World
	
	}
}
